title: Heroin: The Drug
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss heroin: how it is made from morphine and opium, its addictiveness and withdrawal, overdose risks including respiratory depression and fentanyl-laced supply, and its history from Bayer's 1898-era marketing as a trade name through the Harrison Narcotics Tax Act, the opium supply chain (Afghanistan, Mexico, Golden Triangle), the effect of the COVID-19 pandemic on smuggling, marijuana as a supposed gateway drug, and the opioid epidemic rooted in OxyContin reformulation. Opens with a book announcement and movie talk (Trainspotting, Requiem for a Dream, Pulp Fiction) and closes with listener mail about peanut butter color perception.

segments.title: Book announcement and opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts announce the upcoming Stuff You Should Know book and introduce the episode, then banter about drug movies, contrasting weed, cocaine, and heroin films.

segments.title: Heroin, morphine, and effects
segments.summary: Discussion of heroin's relationship to morphine, the difference in duration and addictiveness, and the film Requiem for a Dream and its depiction of injection-site injuries like wound botulism and abscesses.

segments.title: Purity, cutting, and forms of heroin
segments.summary: Heroin's purity and adulterants, black tar heroin from Mexico, cheese heroin, and the forms it can be sold in, including salt, and routes of use.

segments.title: Heroin withdrawal and dopamine
segments.summary: Explanation of the rapid onset of withdrawal, the brain chemistry behind dopamine and tolerance, and how withdrawal can be dangerous via dehydration and electrolyte imbalance. Discussion of Trainspotting's kicking scene and medical treatment with methadone or buprenorphine.

segments.title: Heroin overdose and respiratory depression
segments.summary: Heroin's effect on breathing, which can lead to hypoxia and death from overdose, and the greater danger of heroin compared with withdrawal itself.

segments.title: History: morphine, Bayer, and the name heroin
segments.summary: Opium's long medical history, isolation of morphine, morphine addiction after the Civil War, C. R. Alder Wright's acetylation producing diacetylmorphine, and Heinrich Dreser at Bayer who named it heroin and marketed it as non-habit-forming.

segments.title: Early regulation and the Harrison Narcotics Tax Act
segments.summary: Early warnings from 1906 and 1909, the 1912 Hague International Opium Convention, and the Harrison Narcotics Tax Act, which criminalized drug use and led to the drug war and arrests of doctors treating addiction.

segments.title: Global opium supply and the drug war
segments.summary: Why heroin is hard to eradicate: easy processing and poppies growing widely. Covers the opium supply history in China, the Golden Triangle, the Golden Crescent and Afghanistan, the Taliban's effect on production, and that US heroin largely comes from Mexico and Colombia.

segments.title: Pandemic smuggling, drug mules, and the human cost
segments.summary: COVID-19 pandemic restrictions may be disrupting heroin smuggling and causing a drought that could push users toward meth. Hosts discuss drug mules and the coercion of smugglers, and an anecdote about Kamal Anjohnny's heroin joke.

segments.title: Marijuana as gateway, jazz, and the opioid epidemic
segments.summary: Marijuana as a possible gateway to heroin through jazz musicians in the 1940s and 1950s, heroin in jazz history, fentanyl-laced heroin, and the rise of heroin after OxyContin reformulation and the 2008 recession.

segments.title: Listener mail: peanut butter color
segments.summary: A listener from Louisville shares that peanut butter colored green was a childhood belief, linking to the color blindness episode. Hosts read the email and recommend sending in listener mail.
